\subsection{Adjacency Graph Pruning}
\label{sec:ablation-pruning}

We iteratively refine the adjacency graph used to prune the search space
of the HK2017 algorithm, starting from the unpruned baseline and adding
strictly stronger conditions at each step. Each variant is tested on a
fixed dataset of 38 polytopes to verify correctness and measure speedup.

\paragraph{Variants.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation-variants} lists the four adjacency-graph variants.
Each adds a necessary condition for the existence of a valid orbit transition
$F_i \to F_j$, building on all previous conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lp{9cm}}
\toprule
Variant & Pruning condition for transition $F_i \to F_j$ \\
\midrule
A0 & None (unpruned): exhaustive search over all $(S, \sigma)$ \\
A1 & Vertex adjacency: $F_i \cap F_j \neq \varnothing$, checked via shared polytope vertices (Corollary~\ref{cor:adjacency-pruning}) \\
A2 & Directed $\omega_0$: A1 and $\omega_0(n_i, n_j) \ge 0$, ensuring the Reeb flow on $F_i$ carries the orbit toward~$F_j$ \\
A3 & Reeb-flow feasibility: A2 and $\exists\, x \in F_i \cap F_j$ with $x - \varepsilon R_i \in F_i$ and $x + \varepsilon R_j \in F_j$, ensuring other halfspaces do not block the transition \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Adjacency graph variants, each strictly stronger than the previous.
  The pruning condition applies to each consecutive pair in a candidate ordering
  $\sigma$; orderings that violate any edge condition are discarded.}
\label{tab:ablation-variants}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Directed symplectic condition (A2).}
For a physical orbit transition $F_i \to F_j$ at a ridge point $x \in F_i \cap F_j$,
the backward Reeb flow $x - \varepsilon R_i$ must remain in~$K$.
Checking the half-space constraint for facet~$j$ gives
$\omega_0(n_i, n_j) \ge 0$ as a necessary condition;
the forward flow $x + \varepsilon R_j$ on~$F_j$ gives the same condition
by antisymmetry of~$\omega_0$.
This is condition~(1) of Lemma~\ref{lem:transition-feasibility} below,
which proves the condition is both necessary and sufficient
(together with an LP feasibility check on the blocking set).

\paragraph{Reeb-flow feasibility (A3).}
A3 strengthens A2 by also checking the half-space constraints of all \emph{other}
facets $F_k$ ($k \neq i, j$).
For each $k$, we define a ``blocking set''
$B = \{k \notin \{i,j\} : \omega_0(n_i, n_k) < 0 \text{ or } \omega_0(n_j, n_k) > 0\}$,
and check whether $F_i \cap F_j$ contains a point satisfying
$n_k \cdot x < h_k$ for all $k \in B$.
This is a linear feasibility problem on the 2-dimensional ridge,
solved via Fourier--Motzkin elimination.
The $O(F^4)$ precomputation cost is negligible compared to the exponential search.

\paragraph{Transition feasibility.}
We now characterize exactly when a piecewise-linear orbit can
transition from~$F_i$ to~$F_j$.
Write $R_k = J_0 n_k$ for the characteristic direction on~$F_k$.
In coordinates $(q_1, q_2, p_1, p_2)$ with
$J_0 = \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -I_2 \\ I_2 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$,
we have $R_k = (-n_k^{(3)}, -n_k^{(4)}, n_k^{(1)}, n_k^{(2)})$
and $n_k \cdot R_\ell = \omega_0(n_\ell, n_k)$.
A transition $F_i \to F_j$ requires a point $x \in F_i \cap F_j$
and $\varepsilon > 0$ with
$x + t\, R_i \in K$ for $t \in [-\varepsilon, 0]$
and $x + t\, R_j \in K$ for $t \in [0, \varepsilon]$.
The following lemma shows that the A3 feasibility check
captures this condition exactly.

\begin{lemma}[Transition feasibility]
\label{lem:transition-feasibility}
Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be a convex polytope with facets
$F_1, \ldots, F_N$, outward unit normals~$n_k$, and support values~$h_k$.
Define the blocking set
$B = \{k \notin \{i,j\} : \omega_0(n_i, n_k) < 0
  \textup{ or } \omega_0(n_j, n_k) > 0\}$.
A physical orbit transition $F_i \to F_j$ is feasible if and only if
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\omega_0(n_i, n_j) \ge 0$, and
  \item $\exists\, x \in F_i \cap F_j$ with
    $n_k \cdot x < h_k$ for all $k \in B$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Throughout, we use $n_k \cdot R_\ell = \omega_0(n_\ell, n_k)$.

\emph{Necessity.}
Let $\gamma(0) = x \in F_i \cap F_j$ realize the transition.
For the approach ($\gamma(t) = x + t\, R_i$, $t < 0$),
$n_j \cdot \gamma(t) = h_j + t\, \omega_0(n_i, n_j) \le h_j$
forces $\omega_0(n_i, n_j) \ge 0$ (since $t < 0$),
and the departure gives the same by antisymmetry. This is~(1).
For~(2), suppose $k \in B$ with $\omega_0(n_i, n_k) < 0$.
Then $n_k \cdot (x + t\, R_i) = n_k \cdot x + t\,\omega_0(n_i, n_k)$;
since $\omega_0(n_i, n_k) < 0$ and $t < 0$, this equals
$n_k \cdot x + |t|\,|\omega_0(n_i, n_k)| > n_k \cdot x$.
If $n_k \cdot x = h_k$, this exceeds~$h_k$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$,
violating $\gamma(t) \in K$.
Hence $n_k \cdot x < h_k$.
The argument for departure-blocking $k$ (with $\omega_0(n_j, n_k) > 0$)
is analogous.

\emph{Sufficiency.}
Given $x \in F_i \cap F_j$ satisfying~(1) and~(2),
set $\delta = \min_{k \in B} (h_k - n_k \cdot x) > 0$.
For non-blocking $k \notin B \cup \{i,j\}$:
the approach satisfies
$n_k \cdot (x + t\, R_i) = n_k \cdot x + t\,\omega_0(n_i, n_k) \le n_k \cdot x \le h_k$
since $t \le 0$ and $\omega_0(n_i, n_k) \ge 0$;
the departure satisfies
$n_k \cdot (x + t\, R_j) = n_k \cdot x + t\,\omega_0(n_j, n_k) \le n_k \cdot x \le h_k$
since $t \ge 0$ and $\omega_0(n_j, n_k) \le 0$.
For blocking $k \in B$, the slack~$\delta$ absorbs the perturbation:
choosing $\varepsilon < \delta / \max_k(|\omega_0(n_i, n_k)| + |\omega_0(n_j, n_k)|)$
ensures all constraints hold.
The cases $k = i$ and $k = j$ follow from~(1) and
the antisymmetry $\omega_0(n_i, n_i) = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Ridge sufficiency]
\label{cor:ridge-sufficiency}
If\/ $F_i \cap F_j$ is a 2-dimensional face (ridge) of~$K$
and $\omega_0(n_i, n_j) \ge 0$, then the transition $F_i \to F_j$
is feasible.
In particular, the A2 and~A3 conditions are equivalent
for simple polytopes and for Lagrangian products of convex polygons.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
If $F_i \cap F_j$ is a ridge, any $x$ in its relative interior satisfies
$n_k \cdot x < h_k$ for all $k \notin \{i,j\}$ (hence for all $k \in B$),
so condition~(2) of Lemma~\ref{lem:transition-feasibility} holds
automatically.
For simple 4-polytopes, each vertex lies on exactly four facets,
so any two adjacent facets share a ridge.
For Lagrangian products $P \times Q$ of convex polygons,
each vertex $(v_P, v_Q)$ lies on exactly two edges of~$P$
and two edges of~$Q$, hence on exactly four facets;
thus $P \times Q$ is simple, and every pair of intersecting facets
shares a 2-face (``vertex $\times$ polygon'' or ``edge $\times$ edge'').
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Non-simple polytope where A3 prunes beyond A2]
\label{ex:a3-prunes}
Consider the ``shaved hypercube''
$K = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^4 : -2 \le x_i \le 0 \;\forall\, i,\;
x_2 \le x_1 \,\}$.
This polytope has $9$ facets and $12$ vertices, of which $8$
are non-simple (lying on $5$ facets).
The facets $F_1\colon (x_2 \le 0)$ and $F_2\colon (x_3 \le 0)$
share only a 1-dimensional edge:
the shaving constraint $x_2 \le x_1$ combined with $x_1 \le 0$
forces $x_1 = x_2 = 0$ on $F_1 \cap F_2$.
Since $\omega_0(n_1, n_2) = 0 \ge 0$, condition~(1) holds.
However, the shaving facet~$F_4$ has normal $(-1, 1, 0, 0)/\sqrt{2}$
and belongs to the blocking set~$B$
(since $\omega_0(n_2, n_4) = 1/\sqrt{2} > 0$).
Since $F_4$ is tight on the entire edge $F_1 \cap F_2$,
condition~(2) fails: A2 allows $F_1 \to F_2$, but A3 correctly blocks it.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:transition-feasibility}, no orbit can make this transition.
In total, A3 prunes 8 directed edges that A2 allows.
\end{example}

\paragraph{Correctness.}
All four variants return identical capacities on all 38 test polytopes (maximum
absolute difference $< 10^{-8}$).
This confirms that no pruning variant discards the optimal orbit on this dataset.

The three regression cases additionally verify correct handling of degenerate
KKT systems:
$\triangle{\times}\square$ at $\theta{=}0^\circ$ (expected $3\sqrt{2}/2 \approx 2.121$) and
$\square{\times}\square$ at $\theta{=}0^\circ$ (expected $2.0$) both require a null-space search
when the LU factorization detects rank deficiency;
the hypercube (expected $4.0$) is solved by the LU fast path without SVD.
All three capacities match their expected values to within $10^{-6}$.

\paragraph{Pruning effectiveness.}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation-iterations} shows the number of candidate orderings
$(S, \sigma)$ admitted by each adjacency filter for three $F = 8$ polytopes.
Without pruning (A0), every polytope with $F$ facets admits
$\sum_{m=2}^{F} \binom{F}{m} \tfrac{(m-1)!}{2}$ candidates;
for $F = 8$ this is $16\,064$.
Vertex adjacency~(A1) prunes $59$--$65\%$ of candidates.
The directed $\omega_0$ condition~(A2) provides the dominant reduction,
admitting less than $1\%$ of A0 candidates for generic polytopes
(146 out of $16\,064$) and ${\sim}3\%$ for Lagrangian products.
The hypercube, whose high symmetry produces many $\omega_0 = 0$ pairs,
is the least prunable at $12\%$.

A3 admits exactly the same candidates as A2 on all 38 test polytopes.
All test polytopes are simple (every vertex on exactly four facets),
so every adjacent pair shares a ridge; by Corollary~\ref{cor:ridge-sufficiency},
the $\omega_0$ condition alone guarantees feasibility at ridges,
making the LP check~(A3) redundant.
Figure~\ref{fig:ablation-timing} shows the corresponding computation times.

\midrule
Random generic ($F = 8$)     & 16\,064 & 6\,543 & 146   & 146   \\
Lagrangian $4 \times 4$ ($F = 8$) & 16\,064 & 5\,556 & 497   & 497   \\
Hypercube ($F = 8$)          & 16\,064 & 5\,556 & 1\,970 & 1\,970 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Number of candidate orderings $(S, \sigma)$ admitted by each

  the directed $\omega_0$ condition~(A2) eliminates $87$--$99\%$

  A2 and A3 agree on all test polytopes (all simple).}
